title: Longest Common Prefix
statement: Write a function to find the longest string that is a prefix of every string in an array. If there is no common prefix, return the empty string "".
realWorld: Collapsing a set of paths or URLs to their shared root — what a file browser does to show 'you are in /var/log/app', what a CDN does when deciding a cache-invalidation prefix, and what a router does when summarising a block of addresses into one route.

examples.explanation: All three begin f,l. At the third character "flower" and "flow" have 'o' while "flight" has 'i', so the agreement ends after two characters.
They disagree at the very first character, so the common prefix is empty. Note this is a valid answer, not a failure.
Six characters shared. The answer is bounded by the shortest string, which here is longer than the answer.
The shortest string ends first. A common prefix can never be longer than the shortest input, so the scan must stop there.

constraints: strs[i] consists of lowercase English letters only
An empty string may appear in the array, in which case the answer is ""

bruteForce.idea: Horizontal scanning: take the first string as a candidate prefix and shrink it by one character at a time until every other string starts with it.
code: public static String longestCommonPrefix(String[] strs) {
if (strs.length == 0) return "";
String prefix = strs[0];
for (int i = 1; i < strs.length; i++) {
while (!strs[i].startsWith(prefix)) {      // re-compares the same leading chars
prefix = prefix.substring(0, prefix.length() - 1);   // a new String each time
if (prefix.isEmpty()) return "";
return prefix;

complexity.time: O(S) comparisons in the best case but O(S · L) work in the worst, where S is the total number of characters and L the prefix length

bruteForce.whySlow: Each `startsWith` re-compares the candidate from character 0, so a prefix that shrinks one character at a time re-reads the same leading characters L times over. Worse, `substring` allocates a fresh String on every shrink — so a case like ["aaaa…a", "aaaa…b"] does quadratic character work and allocates L strings to discover a single mismatch that the first pass could have seen. The algorithm keeps asking a question it has already answered.

patternIdentification: This is the trie lesson's idea without the trie object. Imagine inserting every string into a prefix tree: the words share a single chain of nodes for as long as they agree, and the moment two of them differ that chain branches. **The longest common prefix is exactly the path from the root down to the first node that has more than one child, or that ends a word.** Seeing that tells you two things at once — that you should compare the strings *column by column* rather than string by string, and that you can stop the instant a column disagrees or the shortest string runs out. You do not need to build the trie; the vertical scan walks the same spine for free.

optimized.idea: Vertical scanning. Fix a character position, compare that column across every string, and stop at the first disagreement or at the end of the shortest string. This walks exactly the trie's single-child spine: one pass, each character read at most once, no allocation until the answer is cut. When you need the answer repeatedly against a changing query rather than once over a fixed array, build the actual trie instead and walk down while `children.size() == 1 && !isWord` — same spine, amortised over many queries.
code: * Vertical scan: compare column 0 across all strings, then column 1, and so on.
* This is the trie's single-child spine, walked without building the trie.
* O(S) worst case where S is the total number of characters; O(1) extra space.
public static String longestCommonPrefix(String[] strs) {
if (strs == null || strs.length == 0) return "";
for (int column = 0; column < strs[0].length(); column++) {
char expected = strs[0].charAt(column);
for (int i = 1; i < strs.length; i++) {
// The shortest string ends the prefix — a trie node with no child here.
if (column == strs[i].length() || strs[i].charAt(column) != expected) {
return strs[0].substring(0, column);   // one allocation, at the end
return strs[0];   // strs[0] is itself a prefix of every other string

complexity.time: O(S) worst case, where S is the total number of characters; in practice it stops at the first mismatched column, so the typical cost is O(strs.length × answer length)
complexity.space: O(1) extra — a single substring is allocated for the result

commonMistakes: Indexing past the end of a shorter string. The common prefix can never exceed the shortest input, so the column loop must check `column == strs[i].length()` before calling `charAt` — otherwise ["ab","a"] throws StringIndexOutOfBoundsException.
Returning null or throwing when there is no common prefix. The empty string is the correct answer for ["dog","racecar"], and callers rely on it.
Shrinking a candidate with `substring` inside a loop. Each call allocates and copies, turning an O(S) problem into quadratic character work plus L allocations.

Building an actual trie for a single query. It is the right mental model and the wrong implementation here: constructing the trie costs O(S) time *and* O(S) space, while the vertical scan gets the same answer in O(S) time and O(1) space. Build the trie only when many queries will amortise it.

Sorting the array and comparing only the first and last strings. This is a legitimate trick — lexicographic extremes bound the common prefix — but it costs O(S log n) for the sort, which is worse than the linear scan; offer it as an alternative, not as the optimisation.
Ignoring an empty string in the input. One "" forces the answer to "", and a loop that only compares non-empty strings will miss it.
